item.title: Avoid These 5 Types of Emotional Manipulation
item.description:
Emotions

Avoid These 5 Types of Emotional Manipulation

How to tell the difference between emotional manipulation and negative feedback.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • While negative feedback may feel unpleasant, it provides information and guidance to benefit the recipient.
  • Emotional manipulation, however, uses techniques to make someone feel bad intentionally to benefit the user.
  • Thus, manipulation often involves selfishness, disrespect, criticism, withdrawal, and diminishing others.

Sometimes, during social interactions, people hurt each other’s feelings or trigger negative emotions. In those instances, it can be difficult to distinguish between someone providing genuine and necessary negative feedback versus being intentionally hurtful for purposes of emotional manipulation. Fortunately, research into the strategies we use to change the feelings of others (known as Controlled Interpersonal Affect Regulation Strategies) can help us tell the difference. So, below, we will look at some of those strategies—and the details that can help you tell them apart!

Understanding Negative Affect Regulation Strategies

Niven, Totterdell, and Holman (2009) published a foundational article exploring the ways individuals influence each other’s emotions. Through that exploration, they obtained 955 examples of what they called interpersonal affect regulation strategies. Those examples were then grouped into a hierarchy of categories.

At the highest level, strategies were split between those that improved the emotions of others (Affect-Improving) and those that made someone’s mood worse (Affect-Worsening). From there, the affect-worsening strategies were split into the following two categories and seven sub-categories:

The first category, Negative Engagement Strategies, requires confronting someone about a negative situation or emotional outcome, which often makes them feel bad (e.g., expressing disappointment when someone has failed to reach a deadline). These are the strategies we often label as providing negative feedback. They can take two different forms:

  • Affective Engagement involves explaining to someone why they have made you feel bad or how they have hurt someone else. This strategy challenges their behavior and helps them identify the consequences of their actions.
  • Behavioral Engagement addresses someone’s behavior more directly by highlighting their lack of effort, missed deadlines, or forgetfulness. This strategy may also involve putting them under pressure or requiring remedial tasks to make up for the poor behavior.

The second category, Rejection Strategies, involves behaviors that communicate rejection and snubbing someone (e.g., being obnoxious and intentionally hurtful). These are the strategies that we tend to label as emotionally manipulative. They can take five different forms:

  • Putting One’s Own Feelings First (Selfishness) is defined by acting annoyed, sulking around, or being condescending toward other people. This strategy weaponizes and prioritizes personal feelings, while rejecting and controlling the feelings of others.
  • Disrespect utilizes being rude, unfriendly, insulting, or obnoxious to make unrealistic demands of someone else. This strategy uses confrontation to manipulate someone for personal gain.
  • Criticizing involves pointing out someone’s personal flaws, often through nasty comments. This strategy blends being unsympathetic and belittling to manipulate others through criticism.
  • Withdrawal encompasses refusing to talk, reply, or give attention to someone else as a way of punishing them. Essentially, this strategy is giving someone the “silent treatment” until they feel bad and comply.
  • Diminishing Comparison entails bragging, exaggerating, and inflating personal accomplishments to make someone else feel worse by comparison. This strategy creates the perception of a superiority/inferiority difference to influence others.
article continues after advertisement

Avoiding Emotional Manipulation

As we can see from the above categories, there is a big difference between Negative Engagement (i.e., negative feedback) and Rejection Strategies (i.e., emotional manipulation). On one hand, although it can be emotionally unpleasant, negative engagement is ultimately in the service of helping the recipient improve their behavior and make better choices. On the other hand, rejection strategies are hurtful on purpose, to emotionally coerce the recipient for the benefit of the user only. In fact, we can tell the difference by simply looking at the intention behind each strategy—and whether the feelings of the receiver or user are put first.

Beyond rejection and emotional manipulation being solely focused on the user’s own needs, however, it can also be identified by its selfishness, disrespect, criticism, withdrawal, and diminishing comparisons toward the target of manipulation too. Therefore, if an individual is using any of those five strategies to coerce someone for their own gain, especially at that other person’s expense, then it is a clear sign of manipulation (rather than negative feedback). It is also an indication that the specific professional interaction or social relationship is not intended to be fair or mutually satisfying. Furthermore, as I share in my book Attraction Psychology, that type of emotionally coercive behavior is a sign of a bad romantic relationship as well (Nicholson, 2022).

In contrast, while also potentially unpleasant, negative feedback ultimately points toward a resolution that benefits the recipient and strengthens the relationship. Put simply, it gives someone a path toward forgiveness and reconciliation, although they may need to work for it. Therefore, it is based on fair rewards for good behaviors, which eventually improves the feelings of all involved. As a result, it pays to engage with others, even when feedback is a bit uncomfortable—but be sure to avoid the signs and types of rejection and manipulation when you do too!

item.title: The Artifact of Thought
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Artifact of Thought

Is AI driving a disconnect between the poem and the poet?

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Writing was long treated as an artifact proving a mind behind it.
  • AI now creates the same artifacts from a different architecture.
  • This forces us to question how we recognize thought itself.
Source: Image by mleonascimento0 from Pixabay.

It's really rather simple. A poem once seemed to imply a poet. A mathematical proof implied a mathematician. An elegant argument suggested someone doing the arguing. But now, it's getting complicated by artificial intelligence. We can now encounter the artifact of thought without knowing what kind of cognitive architecture (if any) produced what we recognize as thinking.

I want to focus on the word artifact. Recently, I used it in a casual conversation about education. We were talking about writing and learning, and I described a student’s essay as an artifact or proxy of learning. That seemed straightforward and carried the stamp of logic. We can’t actually see learning, so we look at what the student produces and make some reasonable judgment about what happened in that student’s mind. And in that context, we craft that into a single letter grade.

The conversation stopped, but my thinking continued. If an essay can be an artifact of learning, perhaps writing itself can be understood as an artifact of thought. And that creates a much more interesting problem.

Thoughts and the Thinker

Thought is surprisingly difficult to get our hands around. I can tell you what I’m thinking and even work through a problem in front of you with a good old fashioned pen and paper. But the thought, yours and mind, remains curiously inaccessible. What you encounter is its expression—a derivative of sorts. And from that expression you reason backward toward the cognition that produced it.

Writing makes this particularly clear. When I read a beautiful paragraph, I almost automatically imagine a person or even a mind behind it. Someone selected the words, seeks the rhythm and probably shifts direction a few times. Maybe the writer struggled with a sentence or discovered halfway through that the original idea wasn’t quite right. I don’t consciously reconstruct any of this. I simply assume the words carry some trace of the thinking that produced them.

The same thing happens all the time, from a mathematical proof to a clever joke. We embrace the result and form some impression of the intelligence behind it. There’s a lot packed into that little cognitive leap, and until recently there wasn’t much reason to examine it and we just left it alone.

But today, AI gives us a reason.

Recognizing Another Mind

Now, I can encounter an extraordinary paragraph without knowing if someone struggled with it for days or if it just appeared on a screen with the mechanical click of a button. Its quality and meaning can still be there but it becomes harder to reconstruct the cognitive story that preceded the paragraph.

article continues after advertisement

So, here's the question, and one that might be essential for our times. How do we know when someone else is thinking?

When another person speaks or writes, I can recognize something that seems connected to my own interior experience. Someone says something insightful and I make an inference about the person who said it. She’s smart. He understands the problem. That’s a great idea. Language becomes evidence of another mind because we assume some relationship between the expression and the cognitive process that lives behind it.

AI introduces another source of language into that equation, and its architecture is profoundly different from ours. It can produce an observation that surprises us or craft an argument that changes the direction of a conversation. Whatever we ultimately decide about whether AI thinks or understands, something consequential has already happened and it demands our attention. Artifacts we associate with cognition can now emerge from something very different from a human brain.

AI as a Cognitive Contrast Agent

Maybe AI is a sort of cognitive contrast agent. In medicine, a contrast agent helps reveal structures that were already there but difficult to see such as blood vessels. AI may be doing something similar to our understanding of thought. By giving us another architecture capable of producing artifacts that overlap with our own, it begins to expose assumptions that were difficult to notice when human cognition was essentially our only reference point.

We see intelligent behavior and infer intelligence. We encounter a meaningful sentence and infer understanding. We see something creative and imagine creativity somewhere behind it. These inferences feel natural because they were built around the human example. For a long time, there was little reason to separate the artifact from the presumed cognitive process behind it.

article continues after advertisement

AI is changing this as it puts pressure on that relationship because the same outward signal can now have a very different history. This is also why the argument over whether AI “really thinks” may be too narrow. We don’t need to settle that question to recognize what has already changed. AI has complicated the relationship between intelligent expression and the assumptions we make about its source.

And perhaps this is the part I find most interesting. A poem can still move me. A proof can still strike me as brilliant. An argument can still change the way I see something. The artifact hasn’t necessarily lost its power. It's become less revealing about the process that brought it into existence.

What Was the Artifact Telling Us?

We have never had direct access to another person’s thought. We've had all sort of "stuff" that lives at a distance. Words, gestures, ideas, creations are the traces that minds leave in the world. From those traces, we constructed our understanding of other minds. And I think we became so accustomed to making that inference that we rarely noticed we were making it at all.

AI gives us a new kind of trace with a very different origin. And suddenly something that once seemed fairly obvious becomes less so. A beautiful sentence remains a beautiful sentence. But what exactly does its existence allow us to conclude about what happened before it appeared?

Maybe AI will eventually tell us something profound about artificial intelligence. I’m beginning to suspect that one of its more interesting contributions may be what it forces us to reconsider about our human cognition. The artifact is still right there in front of us. What lies behind it has become much harder to locate, and I’m not sure we (yet) understand what that does to the way we recognize thought when we see it.

item.title: What if Our Humanity Is the Key to Exceptional Performance?
item.description:
Sport and Competition

What if Our Humanity Is the Key to Exceptional Performance?

Rethinking what it takes to do extraordinary things.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • High-performance cultures can teach us that sacrifice is necessary for excellence.
  • Not all discomfort is the same; some comes from growth, while some is created by the systems around us.
  • Humanizing high performance is not asking less of people, but creating conditions that allow them to thrive.

For much of my life, I thought I understood what high performance required. As an elite athlete, I learned to devote my mind, body, and spirit to the pursuit of excellence. I learned to be disciplined, to tolerate discomfort, to push through when things were hard, and to keep going when I wanted to stop. There were parts of that experience that I loved, and parts of it that shaped me in ways I remain deeply grateful for.

But there were costs too. Over time, striving for excellence came at a cost to my safety and my psychological and physical health. Some of what I experienced, I now understand, was eroding my humanity. My needs could be put aside, and there was always someone else who could take my place. So I stayed quiet, pushed through, and kept going. Over time, what the environment expected of me became what I expected of myself. For a long time, I understood many of those costs as simply part of what it meant to perform at the highest level.

I do not believe that anymore.

Years later, as an organizational psychologist, I find myself returning to a question I could not have articulated when I was an athlete: Why do we so often assume that the things that make us human are somehow at odds with extraordinary performance?

What We Learn About Excellence

High-performance environments teach us a great deal about what is valued, often without anyone explicitly telling us. Rest can be interpreted as weakness. Fear and uncertainty are hidden. Asking for help can signal that you are not cut out for it. Speaking up can carry consequences. Pain becomes something to push through, and sacrifice becomes evidence of commitment. Eventually, people learn that performing well requires setting aside more and more of themselves.

We do not arrive at these beliefs on our own. We learn them from the environments we grow up in, the places we work, and the stories we inherit about what it takes to be successful. Edgar Schein, one of the most influential thinkers on organizational culture, wrote about how assumptions can become so deeply embedded that we stop recognizing them as assumptions at all. They simply become "the way things are."

Versions of these narratives appear almost everywhere. In sport, we grow up hearing "no pain, no gain" and celebrating the athlete who finds a way to push through. Medicine has historically treated extraordinarily long hours as part of what it means to be a dedicated physician, while in finance and law, working through the night can signal a willingness to do whatever it takes. Tech has its own version of hustle culture, in which exhaustion can become evidence of ambition and commitment. The contexts may look different, but underneath them sits a familiar idea: If something matters enough to us, we should be willing to endure almost anything in its pursuit.

Discomfort Is Not the Same as Suffering

Some of this is easy to confuse with the legitimate demands of excellence.

Doing something extraordinarily difficult is, in fact, difficult. High performance requires focus, discipline, repetition, sacrifice, courage, and the ability to tolerate discomfort. There are moments when performing well means quieting everything else and becoming completely absorbed in the task at hand. I know that feeling intimately, and I believe it is inherently part of the pursuit of excellence.

article continues after advertisement

But there is a difference between discomfort that comes from stretching the limits of our abilities and the suffering created by the systems around us. There is a difference between choosing to sacrifice for something that matters deeply to us and learning that we must sacrifice ourselves to belong.

I certainly did not always recognize that difference when I was an athlete. It was simply what I believed being a champion meant, and what the pursuit of excellence required. When you care deeply about what you are doing, and sacrifice is normalized by the people and culture around you, it becomes remarkably difficult to imagine another way. Perhaps even harder is confronting the reality that giving more of yourself does not guarantee the outcome you are striving for.

The Costs We Don't Always See

What I find myself thinking about now is how easily the pursuit of excellence can begin to take up more and more space, leaving less room for the rest of who we are. Relationships, family, outside interests, and even the time and space we need to rest and recover can gradually become things we learn to put aside in service of the pursuit. Sometimes we do not realize what the pursuit has asked of us until exhaustion has become normal, relationships have received less of us than we wanted to give, or we struggle to remember who we are outside of what we do.

There is a simple analogy I often come back to: When a plant isn't thriving, we don't blame the plant. We look at the conditions around it, asking whether it has enough light, water, and space to grow. Yet in high-performance environments, we often ask people to become more resilient, manage their stress, or recover better, without asking whether the environment itself needs to change.

What Excellence Could Look Like Instead

We already know that constant performance isn't necessarily the path to better performance. Eduardo Briceño calls this the "performance paradox": When we spend all of our time performing, we leave too little space for learning. Getting better requires opportunities to experiment, make mistakes, seek feedback, and practice without every moment being treated as a test.

article continues after advertisement

But I think we need to take that idea one step further. We are not simply performers who occasionally need time to recover so that we can perform again. We are people with relationships and identities, bodies and emotions, interests and lives that extend beyond whatever we are trying to achieve. We need space to recover, to connect, and to have parts of our lives where our worth isn't determined by how well we perform. These things aren't distractions from excellence but part of what allows us to keep showing up with something to give.

I have spent much of my life thinking about what human beings are capable of, first as an athlete trying to find the limits of my own performance and now as a psychologist studying the systems in which people work, learn, lead, and perform.

The more I learn, the less convinced I am that we have reached those limits.

Humanizing high performance is not about asking less of people but about becoming more thoughtful about what we ask of them and why, and creating the conditions for them to bring more of who they are to what they do.

item.title: Procrastination, Let’s Get Straight to the Point
item.description:
Procrastination

Procrastination, Let’s Get Straight to the Point

It’s time to shed some light on how to deal with procrastination and avoidance.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Procrastination and avoidance are subtle, incremental, and often disguised as “busyness.”
  • The first step in dealing with procrastination and avoidance is recognizing it is a choice.
  • By identifying the smallest possible action, you can begin deactivating the procrastination cycle.
Source: Mohamed Hassan / Pixabay

Procrastination and avoidance. There they are, subtle, incremental, and often disguised as “busyness.” Yet in the back of your mind, you know they’re still present. No matter how many distractions you create, the underlying issue remains exactly where you left it; you are procrastinating and avoiding it, whatever it is.

The first step in breaking this self‑imposed choice is recognizing that procrastination and avoidance is a choice. One of the most effective ways to interrupt the pattern is to break the task into its smallest actionable unit.

Why Tasks Feel Overwhelming and How to Break Them Down

Avoidance and procrastination often arise because the task feels too large. By deliberately thinking through the task and identifying the smallest possible action, you have then started the potential to begin deactivating the procrastination and avoidance cycle. If no action is taken, nothing changes. And if thinking does not change, again, nothing changes. And the important point to note here is that thinking and action are choices.

Another strategy is setting a time boundary. When you decide to begin, commit yourself to working for a small, undefined number of seconds or minutes. This can begin by simply physically moving to where the action needs to happen. As the old saying goes, “A thousand‑mile journey begins with the first step.”

The minimum requirement stage is to simply stand. The second stage is to then walk to the starting line. If you’re not at the starting line, you’re not in the race. However, if you are at the starting line, there is at least the possibility of potential.

Standing and being at the starting line is an act of success. The next step is to initiate an action directly connected to the task. Don’t worry about time or anything else. You are here, and you have started; this means you are on your way. Appreciate the fact that you have started, and let time take care of itself.

When this takes place, an emotional response may follow, and it will most likely be positive. Allow yourself to immerse yourself in that feeling, and at the same time—and importantly—stay focused on the task.

Added to this, it is also worth noting that dealing with and overcoming procrastination or avoidance is not about becoming fearless or perfectly disciplined. This is about building a thinking and physical action pattern of small, intentional behaviors that gradually reshape your brain, your thinking, and your behaviors.

article continues after advertisement

Each deliberate choice strengthens the neural connections—and the internal belief—that you can act even when you don’t feel ready. This belief is the foundation of agency. It is also the foundation of self‑trust, to which we can add confidence, which begins the journey in the development of self-regulation and self-management.

When we act—let those words be repeated—when we act, we stop being observers. We become the actors of our own behaviors, self-directed actions, time, and place.

Responsibility Theory and Personal Power Over Procrastination

This also aligns with the statement (in the form of a question and answer) that is in Responsibility Theory: “What am I responsible for, and what power do I have?” The answer is “I am responsible for, and I have power over, what I think, do, say, learn, and choose.” When you are using this power, you are not avoiding anything, and you most certainly are not procrastinating.

The long‑term effect of each self‑initiated choice is cumulative. Avoidance "shrinks" your mind and your world; deliberate action expands both. Avoidance "narrows" your sense of possibility; deliberate action restores it, and it does lead to action potential. Whereas avoidance erodes confidence, deliberate action rebuilds, advances, and enhances confidence, which is connected to an internal locus of control: "I believe in me. I choose my thoughts and actions."

article continues after advertisement

The transformation is not sudden. It is incremental, steady, and grounded in practice. Over time, the pattern becomes stronger; each small act of choice strengthens the self, and procrastination eventually becomes irrelevant.

When you choose to act, you move from thought to something observable. As the saying goes: “I don’t know what you’re thinking, but I can see what you’re doing.” And importantly (with this in mind), what you are doing is to confirm to yourself that you took action, and that you are your own person.

As this unfolds, don’t hold back from celebrating the start. You’re on your way, even if only for seconds or minutes. Again, don’t concern yourself with time; time will take care of itself. What matters is that by taking the first step, you’ve entered the world of action. And that—self‑evidently and irrefutably—means that you are no longer procrastinating or avoiding anything. You are not only in the world of action; you are the action in the world.

This, however, is not the end; neither is it the beginning of the end, or the end of the beginning of anything else of that nature. Procrastination and avoidance will return, and it may do so with a vengeance. And, importantly, this return (of avoidance and procrastination) may even occur immediately after you have completed what you set out to complete.

Even with this taking place, you will have by now advanced with insight and knowledge. One of the direct and to-the-point acknowledgments of the return of procrastination and avoidance is to say the words (either as a whisper, a shout, or just in your mind): “I am procrastinating.” That is because you will have grown in knowledge and experience from what you previously achieved.

Once those words are uttered—"I am procrastinating"—denial no longer exists, avoidance no longer exists, and the action potential of what does exist is to take action against what has now been identified: “I am procrastinating.” So, when I ask the question: "Who's got the power over their procrastination?" Your answer will be strong and confident: "I've got the power over my procrastination."
